input.question: How does a database index speed up queries, and what does it cost?
reference_points: An index is an auxiliary structure, usually a B-tree, that avoids full table scans
Lookups become logarithmic instead of linear
Indexes cost extra storage and slow down writes
input.answer: The index keeps a sorted copy of the key, typically as a B-tree, so the engine jumps to matching rows in log time instead of reading the whole table. The trade-off is extra disk and slower INSERT and UPDATE, because every write also updates the index.

Clients and proxies can safely retry after a timeout
input.answer: PUT replaces the resource with the payload you send, so sending it twice gives the same final state as sending it once. That lets a client retry safely when it does not know whether the first call went through.

input.question: What is the Python GIL and how does it affect CPU-bound threads?
reference_points: The GIL lets only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time
CPU-bound work does not scale with threads; use processes or native extensions
I/O-bound threads still benefit because the GIL is released while waiting
input.answer: CPython has a global interpreter lock, so only one thread runs bytecode at any moment. Number-crunching threads therefore will not use more cores; I switch to multiprocessing or push the hot loop into NumPy or C. For network calls threads are fine since the lock is dropped during blocking I/O.

input.question: How does a database index speed up queries, and what does it cost?
reference_points: An index is an auxiliary structure, usually a B-tree, that avoids full table scans
Lookups become logarithmic instead of linear
Indexes cost extra storage and slow down writes
input.answer: Great question, and it is something I have thought about quite a lot over the years while working with relational databases in different teams and projects. So, to start from the beginning, when you create an index the database builds an additional data structure next to the table, and in most engines, including PostgreSQL, that structure is a B-tree by default. Because this tree is kept sorted, the engine can navigate it and reach the matching rows in logarithmic time, instead of having to go through the entire table row by row, which is what we call a full table scan. Now, of course, nothing comes for free, and there are costs to keep in mind: the index occupies additional storage on disk, and every single time you insert, update or delete a row, the database also has to keep the index up to date, which makes those write operations slower. That is basically the trade-off as I understand it.

input.question: What makes an HTTP PUT request idempotent, and why does it matter?
reference_points: Repeating the same PUT leaves the resource in the same state
Clients and proxies can safely retry after a timeout
input.answer: Okay, so let me walk through this carefully, because idempotency is one of those concepts that people mention a lot in API design discussions but do not always explain precisely. When a client sends a PUT request, it is asking the server to set the resource to exactly the representation contained in the body. What that means in practice is that if the very same PUT request is sent once, twice or ten times, the resource ends up in exactly the same final state every time. And the reason this matters so much is reliability: networks fail, timeouts happen, and a client often does not know whether its first request actually reached the server, so being able to simply retry without worrying about side effects is very valuable.

input.question: Explain the CAP theorem in practical terms.
reference_points: During a network partition a system must choose between consistency and availability
Without a partition both can be provided
input.answer: This is a classic one, and I think it is often misunderstood, so let me take a moment to lay it out in practical terms rather than just quoting the acronym. CAP stands for consistency, availability and partition tolerance. In real distributed systems network partitions are going to happen sooner or later, you cannot really opt out of them, so the interesting part of the theorem is what happens during a partition: at that point the system has to choose between staying consistent, which means refusing some requests, or staying available, which means answering but possibly with stale data. When there is no partition, on the other hand, a well-designed system can provide both consistency and availability at the same time.
